newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euroshares trim loss, Wall St revives, dlr up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euroshares trim loss, Wall St revives, dlr up.

text.p: European stock markets trimmed their losses by mid-afternoon, while Wall Street made a modest recovery in early New York business from its second biggest points loss in history on Friday.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which lost 247.37 points or more than three percent on Friday, opened with moderate gains, slipped into small losses but then revived to show a net rise of around 0.40 of a percentage point after half an hour of trading.

European investors were looking to Wall Street for tips on what to do next amid uncertainty on whether Friday's drop marked an end to a relentless rise in U.S. and European share prices or just a short-term correction.

"We see this as another periodic bout of profit-taking nervousness...There is some froth there to be taken out but nothing fundamental has changed," said Tony Robinson, head of equities at fund manager Lombard Odier.

The revival in shares rubbed off on the dollar, which had earlier suffered jitters over the chance of higher German interest rates in a week with key meetings of monetary policy makers in the United States and Germany.
But gold lost earlier moderate gains and dealers said investors still seemed to lack trust in precious metals as safe financial havens.

After Friday's loss on the Dow, the barometer of U.S. blue-chip stock prices had fallen 6.8 percent from its all-time closing high of 8,259.31 on August 6. But it was still more than 3,000 points or nearly 66 percent above its level two years ago.

Wall Street's fall spurred heavy selling on Monday on Asian markets, many of which are also being undermined by currency turmoil in the region. Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average in Tokyo fell 1.47 percent.

Continental European markets, several closed on Friday for a holiday, were then generally hit more than London, Europe's largest stock market, which had already responded to the early stages of Friday's Dow plunge.
London's FTSE, having opened with a loss of nearly 1.5 percent, was only a third of a percentage point down by mid-afternoon.

The FTSE had tumbled 125.5 points or 2.5 percent on Friday, its largest loss in percentage terms in five years -- but this compared with a much larger plunge of 250.7 points, or 12.22 percent, in the "crash" of October 20, 1987.

In Frankfurt floor trade the DAX index showed an early fall of about four percent but it had closed on Friday before Wall Street's retreat. It later more than halved its loss and the IBIS index revived further in later electronic business.

"We have to remember that the DAX has been a real performer this year and it was time for some sort of a correction," said one Frankfurt dealer, noting that the DAX had gained 55 percent since January while the Dow had added about 30 percent.
Paris, one of a number of markets closed on Friday for Assumption Day, was particularly hard hit with the CAC-40 down some 3.3 percent at one stage before staging a revival to halve its loss.
In contrast, the Amsterdam bourse moved well into the plus column after early losses, gaining around 2.8 percent.
Overall, many market analysts now expect more selective investment strategies to come into favour after a long more general rally driven by the weight of money available.
The dollar recovered to rise back above 1.82 marks after being hit by jitters about higher German interest rates before the Bundesbank holds its first meeting on Thursday after the summer break.
"Fears of knock-on effect today from Friday's (Wall Street) sell-off seem to have been overdone," said Sanjit Maitra, head of economics and strategy at WestLB in London.
"The market's focus is on German rates and a degree of nervousness will persist ahead of the repo tender and the council meeting."

Economists doubt whether the German central bank would move towards higher rates at Tuesday's repo tender or tighten credit after Thursday's council meeting since remarks showing German officials' concern about the mark's decline and inflation have already made an impact.
Markets are also awaiting news from the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee, which meets to consider interest rates on Tuesday but is not generally expected by economists to raise U.S. rates just yet.

The dollar/yen rate pushed higher again but stayed below 118 yen. It had been capped by remarks from U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang who expressed concern about Japanese trade data. Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus jumped almost 70 percent in July.

Analysts, meanwhile, said gold's retreat to 12-year lows this year had taken the shine off the former "safe haven". "They are very wary of gold. It's been a dreadful investment," said analyst Ted Arnold of Merrill Lynch.
"If they are worried about the stock market falling and want a safe haven, they'll go in to cash for a time and then maybe bonds, but it's not going be gold."
CURRENCIES AT 1400 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.8260 marks and 117.83 yen versus 1.8227 and 117.76 in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1400 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE 100 index was down 17.1 points or 0.35 percent at 4,848.7.
FRANKFURT - The DAX index ended floor trade 74.26 points or 1.79 percent lower at 4,078.60. The IBIS index for electronic trade was down just 3.78 points or 0.09 percent at 4,073.81.
PARIS - The CAC-40 index was 39.26 points or 1.34 percent lower at 2,882.58.
The Madrid stock market was down around two percent, Milan 1.9 percent, Stockholm 0.7 percent and Zurich 1.3 percent. The Amsterdam bourse was up 2.8 percent.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $322.60 an ounce, down from a morning fix of $326.05 and Friday's London close of $324.35. Silver gained six cents to $4.51.
